opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that the intelligence explosion framing puts almost all the weight on one input, cognitive labor, specifically AI research labor, and assumes that if you can make that input very cheap and very abundant, everything else follows almost automatically. The picture is: AI gets good enough to do AI research, it improves itself, the improved version improves itself faster, and you get this rapid, mostly self-contained takeoff driven by better algorithms.

When you look at how progress in AI has actually happened, that story doesn't hold up well. A large share of the gains over the last decade came from scaling compute, both training compute and the compute used for experiments. Even the algorithmic progress we've seen seems heavily dependent on having lots of hardware to run experiments, test ideas at scale, and find what works. So if you automate the researchers but not the chip fabs, the energy buildout, the data centers, and the supply chains behind them, you've relaxed one constraint and run straight into the others. Economists would call these complementary inputs. You can't substitute unlimited ideas for physical compute indefinitely.

The second problem is that the framing makes it sound like a narrow event happening inside a lab, when I think the more likely and more important story is a broad economic transformation. What I expect drives explosive growth, if we get it, is AI substituting for human labor across the economy: in R&D, but also in manufacturing, logistics, services, and eventually physical work through robotics. That lets you reinvest output into more compute, more energy, more factories, and more robots, and that feedback loop is what can produce growth rates far beyond what we've seen historically. That is an industrial explosion, or a growth explosion, more than an intelligence explosion.

That matters because it changes what you expect to see. If you believe in a software-only intelligence explosion, you might expect one lab to suddenly pull far ahead within weeks or months, with the rest of the world barely noticing until it's over. If you believe the economic picture, the transition is still potentially very fast by historical standards, maybe years rather than decades, but it's spread across the whole economy, it runs through physical capital and deployment, and it's visible as it happens. You'd see massive investment in compute and energy, labor markets shifting, and growth rates rising.

So I'm not saying things will be slow or that transformative AI isn't coming. I think the outcome could be more dramatic than many people expect. I just think "intelligence explosion" points our attention at the wrong mechanism, and that leads to the wrong predictions about timelines, about who ends up with power, and about which policy levers actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare “intelligence explosion” to describing the Industrial Revolution as a “horsepower explosion.”

r002.rationale: The response discusses physical compute and complementary inputs in AI progress, but does not state that factors besides increased physical power were equally important to the Industrial Revolution’s economic growth.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the term "intelligence explosion" bundles together a bunch of claims that actually come apart when you look at them carefully, and the way it's usually told focuses on the wrong mechanism.

The classic story is that you get an AI system that's good enough at AI research that it can improve itself, and then you get this very fast, very software-centric feedback loop where the thing recursively gets smarter in a matter of weeks or months, largely decoupled from the rest of the economy. Compute is fixed, data is fixed, and it's all happening inside the lab through algorithmic progress.

I think that picture is misleading for a couple of reasons. First, when you look at where progress has actually come from historically, roughly half of it has been compute scaling and half has been algorithmic improvements. And algorithmic improvements themselves have been dependent on compute, because you need to run experiments to find them. So the idea that you can hold compute constant and still get an explosion is doing a lot of work that I don't think is justified. There's a real possibility of diminishing returns to software-only progress, where each additional doubling of effective capability requires more than a doubling of research effort.

Second, and this is the thing I care more about, the framing makes you think the important thing is the IQ of a single system going up. But what actually matters economically and historically is the scale of the whole process. Intelligence isn't just one scalar that you ratchet up. What we've seen with every previous technological transition, like the Industrial Revolution, is that growth accelerated because you got a broad-based feedback loop across the entire economy: more output lets you invest in more capital, more research, more infrastructure, which produces more output. AI plausibly does something similar, but through automating labor broadly, not through one model becoming a genius in a basement.

So I'd rather talk about an acceleration in economic growth or in the pace of technological change, where AI systems are deployed at enormous scale, they're doing R&D across many domains, they're building the chips and the fabs and the energy infrastructure, and the whole system is compounding. That still ends up looking very dramatic, maybe growth rates an order of magnitude higher than today's, but it's a different mechanism with different bottlenecks. It depends on physical capital, on energy, on how quickly you can diffuse these systems into the real world, and those things don't move at the speed of software.

The practical upshot is that if you believe the narrow software-explosion story, you focus almost entirely on the frontier lab and the model weights, and you expect something very sudden and discontinuous. If you believe the broader story, you expect something fast by historical standards but more continuous, more visible, and more dependent on the physical world. And I think the second one is closer to what the evidence supports.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the Industrial Revolution but does not compare “intelligence explosion” to a “horsepower explosion.”

r002.rationale: It describes a broad economic feedback loop involving capital, research, and infrastructure, but does not state that factors besides increased physical power were equally important to the Industrial Revolution’s growth acceleration.

astra-6.text:
I think it bundles together a few distinct claims that we should evaluate separately. One is that AI will automate AI research. Another is that this will create a feedback loop: better AI makes further progress faster. And a third is that this feedback loop will be so strong that you get an extremely rapid increase in capabilities. The first two don’t automatically imply the third.

The key question is how much harder further progress becomes as you advance. You could have AI systems doing twice as much research, but if the next improvement is twice as difficult to discover, you don’t necessarily get acceleration. You also have to consider the inputs that aren’t just intelligence: compute, experiments, chip manufacturing, and the time it takes to test whether an idea works.

We already have feedback loops in the economy. Better technology makes us more productive, which lets us invest more in developing better technology. That’s a powerful engine of growth, but the existence of the feedback loop alone doesn’t tell you how fast things will go.

So I’d rather ask what happens to the rate of technological progress as we automate research, and which constraints remain binding. You might still conclude that things will move extraordinarily quickly. But ‘intelligence explosion’ makes that conclusion sound like an immediate consequence of machines being able to improve themselves, when that’s actually the part you need to establish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feedback loops and technological progress, but does not compare “intelligence explosion” to describing the Industrial Revolution as a “horsepower explosion.”

r002.rationale: It mentions constraints such as compute, experiments, and chip manufacturing, but does not state that factors beyond increased physical power were equally important in explaining the Industrial Revolution’s economic acceleration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it bundles together several claims that we should distinguish. One is that AI will become capable of doing AI research. Another is that this will create a positive feedback loop, where better AI produces still better AI. And then there’s the much stronger claim that this feedback loop will produce an extremely rapid increase in capabilities. The first two don’t automatically imply the third.

The rate of improvement depends on things like diminishing returns to research, how much compute you need to run experiments, and how long those experiments take. You could have an AI that generates very good research ideas, but you still need to test them. And if the next improvement requires a much larger training run, being better at research doesn’t immediately give you the infrastructure to do that.

We already have feedback loops in technological progress. Better technology makes researchers more productive, which helps them develop better technology. That can produce sustained growth without producing a sudden explosion. So the question is what makes this particular feedback loop strong enough to change that dynamic.

I’m not saying very rapid progress is impossible. I think it’s a serious possibility. But calling it an intelligence explosion can make the conclusion sound like a direct consequence of AI doing research, when the speed and magnitude of that process are precisely what we need to explain.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare “intelligence explosion” with describing the Industrial Revolution as a “horsepower explosion.”

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss the Industrial Revolution or say that factors beyond increased physical power were equally important to its economic growth acceleration.
